Anhinga anhinga
ORDER: Suliformes
FAMILY: Anhingidae
Only a snakelike head pokes above the surface as a black body swims silently through a lake. What may appear to be the Loch Ness monster is actually an Anhinga, which swims underwater and uses its daggerlike bill to stab fish. It creates a regal position on the edges of tiny lakes and ponds after each dive, stretching out its silvery wings and holding its head high to dry its saturated feathers. It takes to the sky once it's dry, soaring high on thermals that extend out like a cross. The Anhinga dwells in shallow, slow-moving, protected waters and dries and sunbathing on surrounding perches and banks. Though it may nest on the edges of open bays and lakes, it is rarely found in large stretches of open water. When swimming near the surface, it prefers to stay low in the water, with only the neck and head above the water, and occasionally only the bill. The Anhinga is also a skilled flyer. It flies with its wings flat and straight, its neck outstretched or slightly kinked, and its long, straight tail visible.
